lead.kicker: Ajay Shah reads a wartime economy from space
lead.head: Russia’s economy, lit from above
body: Every night at 1:30 AM, American satellites photograph the Earth. Ajay Shah used those pictures to take on what he called one of the greatest questions of the age: what shape is the Russian economy in?
The answer, from a new paper by Shah and his colleagues, is that it has barely moved. Comparing January with January, Russia’s lights in 2025 were about where they had been in 2019. {#flat}
## A glow that grows

The field began by accident. US government satellites were photographing the world at night for unrelated purposes, Shah said, and “clever analysts started seeing that by mistake you were picking up the light over cities”. As a city prospered, its footprint of light grew.
The idea is easy to love. “Look at the world at night,” Shah said. “And if there is a successful human society down there, it will have lit up the place with light.”
Streetlights, cars and all-night petrol pumps rise with prosperity. So Bandra West glows brighter than Bandra East, and North Korea is dark beside South Korea.
## Handle with care
But Shah, trained at CMIE never to use a measure casually, spent much of the hour on its traps. Nighttime lights, he now says, is far away from GDP: it is a proxy for economic activity. {116-C02}

Testing the data on places they knew, his team found Bombay’s radiance collapsing every July. The few monsoon nights classed as cloud-free, they reasoned, still carried wisps of cloud that dimmed the signal. {116-S03}
Their fix was deliberately conservative: correct only where they were absolutely sure, so that everyone could safely adopt it.
## Enter Russia

Then came Russia. A long war, Shah argued, is a war of economics, won by whoever can keep producing guns, butter and soldiers. Ukraine has Europe behind it. Russia, an Italy-sized economy, has one important patron: North Korea.

Shah, Susan Thomas and Ayush Patnaik held off for years, sure that one of some 500 capable labs would do it. No good paper on Russia appeared. Then, in 2024, Swedish intelligence said Russia’s lights had fallen sharply in 2023, and the team decided to do the work themselves. {116-S04}

Russia broke methods built for India. At 1:30 AM on a summer night in St Petersburg, the sun is shining. Moonlight over the vastness of Siberia added up to false radiance, and the Aurora Borealis lit up Ukraine in 2019.
The findings: war production up, the civilian economy down, the total about flat. Regions near Ukraine are hit by deep strikes, and those near the Baltic states by sanctions. The east is doing fine.
The economy’s centre of mass, Shah said, has moved 245 kilometres east. {116-C10}
Shah now waits for January 2026, when Donald Trump’s easing of sanctions and Ukraine’s improving deep-strike weapons will pull in opposite directions.
Amit Varma, moved to verse three times in the episode, proposed the next topic: other unconventional ways of measuring how a society lives.

second.label: The Second World War
second.head: Poking the giant
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why the Second World War was decided by production
body: When Japan attacked Pearl Harbor and “poked the giant”, Hitler foolishly declared war on America the very next day, Ajay Shah said. Hitler thought he was obliged to. He did not understand America. {116-J17}

Once American production was mobilised, Shah argued, the war was decided. Japan, an island, needed raw materials from across East Asia, and the US Navy strangled its supply chains. Occupied Europe could not match the US, Britain with its empire, and the Soviet Union combined. {116-S06}

Battles still mattered: D-Day could have been lost. But in a long strategic war, Hitler could not compete. Amit Varma doubted anyone understands America even now. “I don’t think America understands America,” he said. {116-J08}

quote.text: And when American production was mobilized on one side, it was really game over.

third.head: The poster he wouldn’t use
body: At NIPFP, Ajay Shah’s colleagues Shekhar Hari Kumar and Shubho Roy were passionate enthusiasts of nighttime lights. They made beautiful maps, and a poster went up in the office.

Shah held back for years. Trained at CMIE, he said, you don’t casually jump into using data: “Either I will have extreme mastery on understanding the innards and the difficulties and the limitations and the trustworthiness of a measure, or I will not use it at all.” {116-S02}
He dived in only when Ayush Patnaik began working inside the VIIRS data with great intensity and effort.
Many economists, he said, simply take the World Bank’s file, which covers all 671 districts of India, and hope “that nothing is bad”. {#districts}

p2.deck: How satellites came to measure prosperity, why the data needs care, and what it reveals about Russia at war

sections.label: The idea
sections.head: The Koreas, after hours
sections.caption: the Korean peninsula at night
body: Nighttime lights began as a by-product, Ajay Shah said: satellites photographing the Earth for unrelated purposes turned out to be picking up the glow of cities, and that glow grew as cities prospered.

He showed the field’s most iconic picture, North and South Korea at night in 2012 and again in 2025, and called it “one of the most influential pictures in the history of the socialism question”. {116-J16}

Answer one to that question, he said, was Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn’s *One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich*. The photograph was answer two. Socialism, he added, should have been tried on hamsters first. {116-R04}
## Free to the world

NASA, NOAA and the European and Japanese space agencies release well-maintained data free to the world, and keep updating it as missions run for ten or twenty years. “This is really glorious,” Shah said. It is measurement without the institutional complexity of a statistics office walking the country. {116-C03}

Because each pixel is small, any boundary can be drawn. His team has added up the light of 300 urban local bodies in Karnataka, a city-level measure that traditional statistics cannot match. {#karnataka}
The data is also monthly, where GDP comes out once a year with a long lag.
~ The reality, Shah warned, is more troublesome: “There’s many a slip between cup and lip.”

quote.text: These are public goods being produced using government money. So it is a statistical system with a twist.

sections.label: The catches
sections.head: Moonlight over Jaisalmer
sections.caption: the limits of the data
body: Ajay Shah walked through what the satellite sees. A forest is dark, and so is the sea, except for ships: a cluster of them waiting at a port reveals congestion. {#ships}
At 1:30 AM a prosperous place has streetlights, compound walls, cars on roads and all-night restaurants. So Bandra West is brighter than Bandra East, and the data shows it.
## Where the light lies
Then come the catches. Go from a one-storey building to a five-storey one, Shah said, and the light does not really increase up there: the roofs trap it. {#storey}
A town that switches to LEDs looks as if it has dimmed. LEDs deliver about 34 per cent less light to the sensor, because much of what they emit does not get through the atmosphere. {#led}
Thick clouds can blot out whole nights; in a July in Maharashtra, almost no light comes through.
On moonlit nights, faint light bounces off empty ground. Added up over an area as big as Jaisalmer, it can match Bandra West, whose GDP is ten times bigger.
~ And near the top, lights stop rising with income: Switzerland and the United States probably look much the same. Economists, Shah said, got a bit over-excited.

quote.text: Nighttime lights is far away from GDP. It’s a proxy for economic activity.

sections.label: The method
sections.head: Garbage in, garbage out
sections.caption: measuring before theorising
body: Half the battle in economics, Ajay Shah said, is measuring something correctly. The analysis and theorising come after. Without depth in measurement, “you’ll just end up doing garbage in, garbage out, and we’re wasting everybody’s life”. {116-C04}
His first test of any dataset is places he knows. Is Bandra West brighter than Bandra East? Is Bandra East brighter than Karjat? If not, “there is some golmaal, something is amiss.” {116-C05}
## The July problem

The test turned up a puzzle: Bombay seemed to go dark every July. NASA and NOAA drop cloudy nights and average the rest, and in July only about three of 31 pass. Shah’s team reasoned that those nights still carried wisps of cloud. {116-S03}

The fraction of cloud-free days, then, could measure the bias. They built a deliberately conservative correction, choosing to undercorrect so that everyone could adopt it safely and leave bolder fixes to later researchers. {116-C06}
Checked elsewhere, it barely changed cloudless Dubai, and added value in cities like Johannesburg, which has a monsoon in part of the year.
~ The paper and a Julia package are public. Amit Varma praised the decision to let anyone play with the data and change its parameters: “That’s a spirit of inquiry.”

quote.text: So we undercorrect, but we are absolutely sure that we are adding value by our undercorrection.

sections.label: The war economy
sections.head: More guns, less butter
sections.caption: strategic war as economic war
body: A long war, Ajay Shah argued, is a battle of economies. Bravery and generals matter, but the economy has to produce the guns, the butter and the able-bodied soldiers. {116-C07}
Ukraine need not produce much. It is backed by Europe, where the guns are made in Germany and the butter in the UK. Russia, an Italy-sized economy, has one important patron: North Korea.
## Four blows

Shah listed the pressures on Russia. One to two million of its most educated and richest people fled. Western sanctions made buying, paying and earning hard. The economy was rejigged towards war production. {116-C08}

Fourth, and newest, are Ukraine’s standoff weapons. In the Second World War, Soviet factories moved deep inland were safe, because Germany never built a long-range bomber. Today Ukraine can hit targets up to 2,000 kilometres inside Russia, more than the distance from Delhi to Bangalore. {#bangalore}
“So imagine there’s a war going on at Delhi,” Shah said. “But there are deep strike weapons coming and hitting near the Karnataka Tamil Nadu border.” {116-C09}
~ These weapons, he said, arrived only in the last six to nine months; the hosts were speaking in August.

quote.text: First, we’ve always known that strategic war is a war of economics.

sections.label: The findings
sections.head: The economy heads east
sections.caption: Russia’s lights, January to January
body: Russia has pulled back on releasing data, Ajay Shah said, “as they should, because that data is strategic”. Satellites fill the gap.
He compares January with January. Russian Januaries are dark at 1:30 AM and free of cloud: “January is the time to peek into the Kremlin.” {116-J09}
War production is up and the civilian economy down. Put together, Shah said, from 2019 to 2025 “the quick answer is about zero change.” {#flat}
## A map in red
On his map of provinces, the regions around the Ukraine border are deep red. Ukraine’s standoff weapons, Shah said, are hitting deep inside Russia.

Regions bordering the Baltic states have suffered from sanctions, as the gains from trade went into reverse. The eastern borders, where sanctions are probably not being enforced, have done reasonably well.
Net net, the centre of mass of the Russian economy has moved 245 kilometres east. {116-C10}
Amit Varma had one last idea: an episode on unconventional metrics, such as rising divorce rates as a sign that women are empowered. {116-C11}
~ Shah is now watching for January 2026: Donald Trump easing sanctions, against Ukraine improving its deep-strike weapons.

quote.text: So the Russian economy is shifting in its character away from the west to the east.

side.boxText: *Shedding Light on the Russia-Ukraine War*, by Rounak Hande, Ayush Patnaik, Ajay Shah and Susan Thomas, reads Russia’s economy from corrected nighttime lights. Its methods paper, *But Clouds Got In My Way*, nods to Joni Mitchell’s *Both Sides Now*. {116-J15}

contQuote.text: I think that’s the core intellectual honesty of being a good economist, which is you must be passionate about measurement. You have to really wage war on measurement.

stories.caption: Bombay’s dark Julys
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the month Bombay vanished from the satellite
stories.head: Monsoon, with a chance of bias
body: Ajay Shah and his colleagues began their work on nighttime lights the way he says everyone should: by checking the data against places they knew. Is Bandra West brighter than Bandra East? Does the light of Bombay add up? {116-C05}
When they plotted the graphs, something jumped out. Bombay’s radiance seemed to collapse every July. {116-S03}

That made no sense. “We know there is absolutely no decline of the GDP of Bombay or the economic activity in Bombay every July,” Shah said. July is the monsoon, so clouds were the obvious suspect, but NASA and NOAA say they work only on cloud-free days.

So the team dug into the method. Each night the satellite takes a picture at 1:30 AM. A separate step classifies it, zero or one, as cloudy or clear. Cloudy nights are thrown away and the rest averaged. Over a pixel in Bombay, that might leave three nights in July.

Two ideas cracked it. The first: “We are from Bombay. We know that there are no cloud free days in July in Bombay.” The second: if a month has 28 cloudy days and three clear ones, the clear ones probably carry wisps of cloud, enough to dim the light.
That made the fraction of cloud-free days a measure of the bias. January, when 25 nights of data out of 31 come through, is genuinely clear; July, with three, is not. {#january}

~ They built an extremely conservative correction and tested it abroad. In Dubai, cloud-free all year, it barely changed anything. In Johannesburg, where there is a monsoon for part of the year, it added value.
stories.why: Great institutions can miss a bias that local knowledge exposes at once. The clue was something any Bombay resident knows: the city is never really clear in July. {116-S03}
stories.postscript: The paper and a Julia package are public. There is no case, Shah said, for anyone to keep using the uncorrected data.

stories.caption: Russia’s midnight sun
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the surprises of studying the biggest country
stories.head: Sunshine at 1:30 in the morning
body: Russia, Ajay Shah found, breaks methods built for India. It is so big that his team struggled to load its satellite imagery into a computer’s memory. They cut it into provinces, and the biggest is still bigger than India. {#province}
The satellites photograph the Earth at 1:30 AM. “You’ll be pleased to know that in the summer at one thirty AM in Saint Petersburg, the sun is shining,” Shah said. {116-S05}

Then there was Siberia. Little dribs of moonlight reflecting off its empty vastness added up to what looked like real radiance. The team’s background-noise algorithms had been tuned for the deserts of Rajasthan, which are small by comparison.
~ Gas flares had to be filtered out too, and in 2019 the Aurora Borealis produced an amazing amount of light over Ukraine.
stories.why: Methods tuned for one country can fail badly in another. Shah’s team caught each trap only by staying close to the data, which is why he told every economist to love their data deeply. {116-J13}

stories.start: Okay, when the war started, I immediately wanted to start doing that.
stories.end: we're going to go study the Russian economy using nighttime lights data.
stories.caption: Swedish intelligence
stories.kicker: Why Swedish intelligence beat the academics to Russia
stories.head: Spies got there first
body: When the war began, Ajay Shah wanted to study Russia with nighttime lights. He, Susan Thomas and Ayush Patnaik held back: it was too obvious, some 500 labs knew the data, and surely the Europeans would do it. {#labs}

So they went back to households in Karnataka. No good papers on Russia’s economy appeared, and the idea, Shah said, kept waking up every three days. Then in 2024 Swedish intelligence said Russia’s lights had fallen sharply in 2023. “Intelligence agencies in advanced economies are using nighttime lights data and the damn academics are not,” Shah said. {116-S04}
“They have skin in the game,” Amit Varma said. Shah agreed, and drew the lesson: “you want to get something done, do it yourself.”
~ It was a struggle, he admitted: the team is grossly under-resourced. But they decided to do it anyway.
stories.why: Don’t assume an obvious piece of research is already being done. People who need an answer to act, like intelligence agencies watching a war, can outrun people who only need it to publish.

stories.caption: the first night pictures
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how a field was born by mistake
stories.head: Born of a happy accident
body: The satellites were never meant for economics. US government satellites were photographing the world at night for unrelated purposes, Ajay Shah said, when analysts noticed they were picking up the light over cities. {116-S01}
Over the years, as a city succeeded and grew, the footprint of its light grew too. That led to a conjecture: could light seen from space tell you about economic activity?

The early data was crude: pixels three kilometres across, the brightest cities top-coded like audio that clips, readings once a year. Then, Shah said, came “a revolution in 2011”, when NASA and NOAA launched the VIIRS sensors. {#revolution}
~ They photograph the world every night at 1:30 AM, in pixels of about 700 to 800 metres, and the pictures are assembled into decent monthly statistics.
stories.why: Whole research fields can grow from the by-products of someone else’s project. The data was there all along; someone just had to look at it with a different question in mind.

quiz.q: What does the famous nighttime picture of the Korean peninsula answer, according to Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: Whether socialism works. It was answer two; Solzhenitsyn’s book was answer one.

quiz.q: Why did Bombay seem to go dark every July in the satellite data?
quiz.a: Its few ‘cloud-free’ monsoon nights still carried wisps of cloud that dimmed the light.

quiz.q: Which month does Ajay Shah compare year on year to study Russia, and why?
quiz.a: January: Russian nights are dark at 1:30 AM and free of cloud.

quiz.q: How far east has the centre of mass of Russia’s economy moved?
quiz.a: 245 kilometres, as the west took strikes and sanctions and the east held up.

quiz.q: Why can’t a 1:30 AM photograph of summer St Petersburg count as night?
quiz.a: Because in summer the sun is still shining there at that hour.

quiz.q: Who said publicly in 2024 that Russia’s nighttime lights had fallen sharply in 2023?
quiz.a: Swedish intelligence, which spurred Shah’s team to study Russia themselves.
